Decision Model Baseline · Champions VGC 2026 Reg Set M-B · experiment menu, 2026-10-25

Jev picks a team

A decision model does one thing. It reads a situation, looks at a list of options you wrote, and returns a probability for every option. Pokémon team building is a long run of exactly those choices. This page lists fourteen ways to test whether a decision model is good at it, and sketches the chart each test would produce.

The model under test is Jev, TypeSafe AI's decision model. It is not a language model: it never writes text, so it cannot misspell a move or invent an item. It can only pick from the list. That makes it a natural fit for the project's fill-in-the-blank task, where a team has some fields hidden and a model must fill them back in.

state · the partial team Jev reads

One team from the scratch team writer's trace, with Swampert's item hidden. In the real run the state is this team as text, with the hidden field marked.

one Choice question · what comes back invented probabilities

instructions Which item should Swampert hold?

Six of the 148 Reg M-B items. Jev returns choice (the top option), confidence, and probabilities for every option sent. The probabilities above are made up to show the shape of the answer.

from typesafe_sdk import Choice, TypeSafeClient

# Reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Model defaults to "jev-latest" (TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL),
# address to https://api.typesafe.ai (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL).
with TypeSafeClient() as client:
	response = client.system_one(
		state={
			"format": "Champions VGC 2026 Reg Set M-B",
			"team": partial_team,  # six slots; hidden fields are None
		},
		questions={
			"swampert_item": Choice(
				instructions="Which item should Swampert hold to do best against the meta?",
				criteria={
					"Leftovers": "Restores 1/16 max HP each turn",
					"Sitrus Berry": "Restores 1/4 max HP at half HP or less",
					# one entry per legal item, at most 255
				},
			),
		},
	)

answer = response.choices["swampert_item"]  # the same object as response.answers[...]
answer.choice         # the option with the highest probability
answer.confidence     # 0 to 1
answer.probabilities  # one value per option, summing to about 1

Code 1. Written against the SDK source at tag v0.7.5: typesafe-ai/typesafe-sdk-python 🟢 (pip install typesafe-sdk, PyPI 🟢). state takes text or a JSON object, so the partial team goes in as structured data. criteria maps each option name to a description, or to None. response.choices is response.answers filtered to Choice answers, so the two spellings in the docs both work. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is the setting a later run would change to point the same code at another decision model.

Which blanks fit in one question

A Choice question takes at most 255 options. Some blanks fit easily, two do not, and other decision models allow far fewer. Pick a blank.

Figure 1. Option counts from code/data/regmb-vocabulary.json and the learnsets (counts recorded 2026-10-24). Limits: Jev 255 (TypeSafe docs), Upstage Solar Decide 26 (its API page), Quyet 10 (its model card). Stat Points are numbers that must sum within a budget, so they are not a list at all.

What Jev is sent

A mask becomes a chain of Choice questions, one per hidden field, asked one at a time. Each answer is written into the team before the next question, so the item question already knows which species was picked. This is the structure decided so far, written before any code exists. It will be replaced by the real printed prompt once the prompt builder is done, and you read that version before any call is sent.

about 17,200 tokens (characters ÷ 4) · Jev's limit is 32,000 per question

    
    
      
  1. meta lists the top-50 meta teams the filled team will battle, the same list Ling's prompt gives it.
    2. 
      
  2. team is the masked team as structured data, with the fields Jev has already filled written in. Hidden fields are None.
    3. 
      
  3. asking_about names the one field this question fills, using the grid's own path names.
    4. 
      
  4. instructions come from one template per field type (below), with the slot number and species filled in. The same wording is used in every run, so the wording test (experiment 13) can vary it on purpose.
    5. 
      
  5. criteria holds only legal options, one rule per field:
        
      
          
    • species: no family already on the team. A whole hidden Pokémon also needs four learnable moves and an ability with an item no teammate holds.
      • 
          
    • ability: one of the species'. Fixed item: legal with it. Hidden item: leaves an item free.
      • 
          
    • item: legal for the species and ability, held by no teammate, and not the only stone another hidden-item Mega needs.
      • 
          
    • move: the species learns it and the slot lacks it.
      • 
          
    • Stat Alignment: any of the 25.
      • 
          
    • Stat Points: a spread seen on that species (training teams and top-50 meta), or one of five generic spreads.
      • 
        
    
        Each option's description is a JSON object of game facts, not prose.
    6.

Figure 2. The request above is real: meta grid unmasked team MB158 with slot 4's item hidden, built from the grid's mask, the meta list Ling's prompt uses, and the simulator's legal items and effect text. Hover a highlighted part to see it in full, click to keep it open. Below are the six question templates, with one example option each. A hidden Pokémon asks all six kinds in this order, four of them for its moves. Option text comes from the Showdown tables in code/data/ and the pinned simulator. The "..." stands for each option's short effect text, which the prompt builder fills in.

  
Three rules sit around the questions:

  
    
    
  • Species tournament. The legal species are split at random into groups of at most 255. Jev answers one question per group, then a final between the group winners.
    • 
    
  • Four runs per mask. One takes Jev's top option at every question. Three sample each answer from Jev's probabilities. Because later questions see earlier answers, each run asks its own questions.
    • 
    
  • 32k tokens per question. The state plus one question must fit. The prompt builder counts tokens for every question and refuses a mask that doesn't fit.
    • 
  

  
Decided: Jev sees the meta. The state carries the top-50 meta teams, as Ling's prompt does, so both models know the opponents. That costs about 12k tokens per question (my estimate: 50 pastes at about 250 tokens each) and leaves about 20k of the 32k limit for the options, so species groups in the tournament are sized by tokens as well as by the 255-option limit.

Where Jev joins the scoreboard

  
Jev gets the same test every other model in this project took: the Mask Lab grids. Each grid starts from five teams, hides parts of them in 270 ways (masks), asks a model to fill each mask, rejects illegal fills, and battles every legal team against the top-50 meta teams. The score is a win rate: the share of battles the filled team wins against the top-50 meta teams, with the behaviour-cloning battle policy playing both sides.

  

    
GridFive unmasked teamsQuestion it answers

    
      
randomrandom legal teams nobody builtCan a fill add strength to a team with the most room to improve?

      
held-outreal teams placed 51 to 100, never trained onDoes a fill hold up on a good team the model never saw?

      
metafive of the top-50 meta teamsCan a fill keep a top team strong, or does it break it?

At $0.042 per million input tokens and about 5,000 tokens per question (my estimate, not measured), that is a few dollars per grid, and roughly three times that with the meta teams in every question. The grid runner's dry run will give the real number. The battles are the larger cost.
    


  
    What is the true performance of Jev so far
    

  
    
    
    "True" here means the held-out grid: five real teams placed 51 to 100, none of them in the top-50 meta list that every Jev question carries. The other two grids each have a catch. On the meta grid the unmasked teams are in that list, so Jev can copy the hidden answer. On the random grid the unmasked teams are random legal teams, so most fills score low: Jev's top pick averages 0.062 there. All three grids ran on 2026-10-27, with the prompt approved in Figure 2b.
    
    
    
      
    3,037 / 3,037Jev fills legal across the three grids. It can only pick options on the legal list.
    
      
    +0.001held-out win rate, Jev's top pick minus the unmasked team, over 270 masks
    
      
    $35.58for 35,987 Jev calls, smoke run included, about 1.2¢ per filled team
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
      
    
      
    
      
    
    
    
    
    Figure 4. Pick a grid and a kind of mask; the number in brackets is how many masks of that kind each grid holds. Each row is Jev's top pick minus another fill, mask by mask, on the masks where both are legal. The dot is the mean difference and the line its 95% interval, from resampling the grid's unmasked teams 4,000 times (five per grid, fewer in rows where an unmasked team has no mask both fills share). A filled dot means the interval clears zero; a hollow dot means it does not. Win rate is the share of battles a filled team wins against the 49 top-50 meta teams, one battle each, with the behaviour-cloning policy on both sides and the slots in listed order. So every team's score rests on 49 battles. A shuffled re-battle of the held-out grid, eight battles per opponent, gives Jev minus Mercury high −0.4 points on the same masks (code/docs/jev-measurements.md). Ling's fills have battle scores on the random grid only. The text writer is the fine-tuned text diffusion model. Means from ~/vgc-data/jev/<grid>-report.json; intervals computed from its per-mask rows.
    

    
    What the held-out grid says
    
    
      
      
    • Jev matches the unmasked teams. Across all 270 masks the top pick is +0.001 [−0.041, +0.047] against the team it was cut from.
      • 
      
    • Jev ties Mercury and always produces a legal team. +0.003 [−0.015, +0.018] on the 183 masks Mercury filled legally. Jev filled all 270.
      • 
      
    • It beats the floor and the text writer. +0.163 over a random legal fill, +0.030 over the text writer.
      • 
      
    • A whole hidden Pokémon is its weak spot. −0.043 against the unmasked team and −0.051 against Mercury, though that second figure covers only 11 masks.
      • 
      
    • Sampling costs strength. Drawing each answer from Jev's probabilities in place of the top pick loses 0.033. From 2026-10-27 the runs send the top pick only, which costs a quarter as much.
      • 
    
    

    
    Copying or choosing?
    
    
    Each cell is the share of hidden fields, across every kind of mask except a whole Pokémon, where the top pick equals the value the mask hid. On the meta grid Jev often reads the answer straight off the meta list, so its fills there measure memory as much as judgement. On the held-out grid every rate drops, yet the win rate holds: where Jev picks something else, it picks something about as strong.

    Other decision models
    
  
    The project runs one decision model, Jev. The code still takes the model's address, name and option limit as settings, so a later run could swap in a different one. That is realistic because many models now copy Jev's request shape (state plus named questions, served at /v1/systemone). The catch is the option limit, which ranges from 10 to 255, so the species tournament from experiment 11 stays in the code whichever model it calls.
